## Overview

The Trobriand are people of the Trobriand Islands whose settlements are primarily based on subsistence horticulture. Their social structure is organized through matrilineal clans that control land and resources. Yams and pigs represent wealth and power and are used as currency, while regional exchange takes place through the *kula* circuit, involving visits to trading partners in seagoing canoes. The people speak Kilivila, an Austronesian language with different dialects among different tribes and a complex system for classifying nouns. Their folk-culture significance in the sources lies in the organization of exchange, yam cultivation, magic, mourning, marriage, food customs, and the transformation of cricket into an aggressive cultural performance after inter-group warfare was banned.

## Material culture

### Clothing & dress

They state that young people attending the delivery of yams to a yam house wear their most festive traditional clothes. During mourning, people closely related to the deceased avoid eating “good food,” while more distantly related people may wear black clothes.

### Architecture

Yams are stored in yam houses. At the beginning of the harvest, yams remain on display in gardens for about a month before being carried to the owner’s husband’s empty yam house.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

They mention seagoing canoes used in the *kula* exchange, yam baskets used to carry produce, books in which literate villagers write magic spells, and bundles of scored banana leaves used as currency among women.

### Jewelry & body adornment

Betel nuts are chewed with pepper plant and slaked lime, and the stimulant commonly causes the teeth to appear red. Beauty magic may be chanted into coconut oil, which is rubbed onto the skin, or into flowers and herbs used to decorate armbands and hair.

## Music & performance

They do describe performance practices connected with yam exchange and cricket. When young people carry yam baskets to the owner’s hamlet, they sing out to announce the arrival of the yams while thrusting out their hips in a sexually provocative way. In cricket, every time a team scores, a special dance ritual is performed. These dances adapt former war rituals and often include taunts and jeers directed at the opposing team. Their words are described as sexual metaphors through which teams taunt one another and display physical and sexual prowess before young women on the sidelines.

Magic is also integrated into cricket strategy. Teams use charms and incantations to gain an advantage, including spells intended to make an opposing team less efficient at scoring.

## Dance & theatre

Cricket became a cultural replacement for war after colonial authorities banned tribal conflict. Matches are generally played between all-male teams and may last several months. The sport incorporates elements understood as reflecting Trobriand culture: there is no limit on team size, special dance rituals accompany scoring, and performances include taunts and jeers. The dances are adaptations of former war rituals and contain sexual metaphors.

## Festivals & rituals

The annual harvest and feasting period is called *Miamala*. At this time, the islanders may still face hunger and scarcity because of poor growing conditions. During the yam harvest, yams remain displayed in gardens for about a month. Their delivery to a woman’s yam house is marked by a ceremony: young people dress in festive traditional clothes, carry yam baskets to the owner’s hamlet, sing to announce the arrival, and perform sexually provocative movements. The yam house owner gives the gardener and young people cooked yams, taro, and pork when the house is loaded. Once the yam houses are full, a man performs a spell intended to ward off hunger by making people feel full.

Marriage has no traditional ceremony in the sources’ account. A woman stays in her lover’s house, and the couple waits for the bride’s mother to bring cooked yams. After the couple eat together for about a year and then return to eating separately, the marriage is officially recognized. A couple may divorce after a year.

Mourning lasts months. The spouse is joined by female kin and the dead person’s father’s sisters. They remain in the house and cry four times a day. Burial exchanges begin the day after burial and involve yams, taro, and small amounts of money.

## Foodways

The main foods named in the sources are yams, taro, and pork. Yams are central not only to subsistence horticulture but also to wealth, power, marriage, kinship, and exchange. Each year, a man grows yams for his sister and, if she is married, for his daughter. A husband does not provide yams to his wife. The number of yams a woman receives is associated with her power and wealth, and a husband is expected to give his wife’s father or brother a gift in return for the yams provided to her.

In ordinary social life, eating in front of others is taboo. People eat alone at their own hearths, turning away from one another and eating rapidly. Betel nuts may be chewed socially, especially with pepper plant and slaked lime. During yam-house ceremonies, the owner gives cooked yams, taro, and pork to the gardener and the young people. Women use bundles of scored banana leaves as currency, exchanging them for canned food or other goods.

## Oral tradition & literature

The Trobrianders practice traditional magic spells, which young people learn from older kin in exchange for food, tobacco, and money. Spells may be directed toward beauty, erotic attraction, or bodily visual and olfactory effects. They are often transmitted only a few lines at a time, and an older person may die before completing the transmission. Trobrianders believe that no one can create a new magic spell. Literate villagers write spells in books and hide them.

Cricket performances include verbal taunts and jeers, whose words are sexual metaphors connected with physical and sexual prowess. Sergio Jarillo’s edited volume *Trobriand Tales, Kwanebuyee Kilivila: Folktales and Mythical Stories from the Trobriand Islands of Papua New Guinea* presents folktales and mythical stories collected by Jerry W. Leach and held at the National Anthropological Archives.

## Language & religion

The Trobriand peoples speak Kilivila, an Austronesian language with different dialects spoken in different tribes and a complex system of classifying nouns. By the 1980s, Trobrianders occasionally spoke Tok Pisin and English, although foreign languages were less commonly spoken. The name “Trobriand” is not Kilivilan; the islands take it from the French explorer Jean François Sylvestre Denis de Trobriand, who visited in 1793.

Traditional beliefs include the idea that pregnancy results from a *baloma*, or ancestral spirit, entering a woman’s body. The mother’s brother, rather than the father, presents a harvest of yams to his sister so the child receives food from its own matrilineage. Most islanders adhere to native tribal traditions. Missionisation has had a mixed effect, and missionaries sometimes attempt to insert Christian blessings into traditional funeral ceremonies.

- Bronisław Malinowski and Dorothy D. Lee are named in the source in connection with the study of Trobriand language and systems of meaning.
